video_title: Cooking with Reducto’s CEO: Why PDFs Still Break AI — Adit Abraham
gist: Reducto CEO Adit Abraham explains why PDFs, designed for printers, remain a hard vision problem for agents, and announces R1, an in-house end-to-end parsing model priced below Reducto's base tier with higher accuracy, plus structured extraction cut from ~4.5 cents to about half per page. He argues post-trained task models beat frontier LLMs on accuracy, cost and latency, frontier models silently fail on recall, and white-collar work has yet to have its 'Claude Code moment' in document editing.

themes.theme: R1 in-house model and cost collapse

insights.claim: Reducto is launching R1, an in-house end-to-end document parsing model that handles both layout capture and last-mile corrections, replacing its earlier pipeline of small traditional CV models plus larger models for hard cases.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Specialist doc-AI vendors are vertically integrating their own models rather than orchestrating third-party ones.
insights.quote: which is our new like in-house model. We're calling it R1

insights.claim: Adit says R1 will cost less per page than Reducto's base models while delivering better accuracy than its most accurate models, making pricing 'multiples cheaper' than before.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Document parsing is on a steep price-deflation curve; per-page pricing power for incumbents is eroding.
insights.quote: it'll be less than the per page cost of our base models >> for better accuracy than our most accurate models.

insights.claim: With R1, Reducto is eliminating pricing multipliers it previously charged for turning on agentic features, simplifying adoption in production.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Simplified flat pricing lowers friction for high-volume enterprise deployment.
insights.quote: So for a while we would have these multipliers if you were turning on aic features and things like that.

insights.claim: Reducto's structured extraction historically cost over 4.5 cents per page all-in, and its newly announced models cut that to roughly half while improving citations performance and schema adherence.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Structured extraction unit costs halving signals rapid commoditization and expanding addressable volume.
insights.quote: historically a page of structured extraction would have cost you all in like over 4.5 cents. And now we're able to do that at half the rate while also improving performance.

insights.claim: Adit says the cost reductions were not a deliberate cost-cutting effort but a byproduct of focusing on performance, yielding better 'intelligence per dollar'.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Task-specific model improvements compound into cost and accuracy simultaneously.
insights.quote: we're just finding that we can get to better intelligence per dollar while happening to just focus on the performance itself.

insights.claim: Reducto processes a little over one billion pages per month, a number Adit says is changing very quickly.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Indicates large and fast-growing enterprise document-processing volume flowing through AI-native vendors.
insights.quote: today reducto processes a little over a billion pages every single month.

themes.theme: Specialized post-trained models vs frontier LLMs

insights.claim: Reducto finds that for a specific task, a post-trained model outperforms frontier foundation models on all three dimensions of accuracy, cost and latency, so its stack has shifted increasingly in-house.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that narrow vertical model specialists can beat general frontier models on unit economics.
insights.quote: if you are looking at a specific type of task, a post-trained model on that task outperforms on all three dimensions.

insights.claim: Adit says frontier foundation models still make sense for genuinely horizontal tasks within Reducto's stack, but that scope is limited today.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Frontier labs' share of specialized enterprise pipelines may shrink as vendors in-source.
insights.quote: There are still like really horizontal tasks where uh Frontier just foundation model makes sense, but >> that's limited in scope today.

insights.claim: Reducto's Deep Extract research found that with uncapped reasoning time, frontier models beat many specialized document platforms on precision, but fail on recall by silently dropping rows and context.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Recall failures are invisible in production, creating a durable need for audit/harness layers on top of frontier models.
insights.quote: But the failure mode for the frontier models was on recall. So they were silently dropping rows um missing bits of context like those sorts of things.

insights.claim: Adit argues missed extractions are especially dangerous because you cannot detect in production what you failed to extract, which is why an auditing harness around model outputs matters.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: The 'just wait for base models' argument underestimates silent recall loss.
insights.quote: like you don't know what you failed to extract in the first place.

insights.claim: Reducto's earlier RolmOCR model was built on top of the Qwen VLM, per the host, before the shift toward fully in-house models with R1.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Open-weight Chinese VLMs served as a base layer for Western doc-AI startups.

insights.claim: Adit likens document understanding to self-driving: lane assist has existed for years, but fully autonomous end-to-end driving like Waymo is a different bar, and that is the bar Reducto targets.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames doc parsing as a long-tail reliability problem rather than a solved OCR problem.
insights.quote: We liken it a lot to self-driving car research.

insights.claim: Adit explains PDFs were designed for printers to faithfully reproduce documents, not for agents to read them, making human-fidelity reading a hard vision problem.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Structural mismatch of the PDF format sustains demand for specialized parsing.
insights.quote: Like the original context for PDF as a file format was for printers to be faithful to the original, right?

themes.theme: Benchmarks, evals and reliability in low-error industries

insights.claim: Adit says benchmarks have largely become marketing material because every vendor is number one on its own benchmark, so Reducto partnered with micro1 for an independent benchmark where Reducto did not choose documents or set ground truth.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Treat vendor-published AI benchmarks skeptically; independent evals and customer trials matter more.
insights.quote: benchmarks largely have become marketing material. M >> um everybody's number one on their own benchmark

insights.claim: Adit says the thing that matters most is for buyers to test tools on their own documents, with independent benchmarks only giving directional signal.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Enterprise doc-AI procurement is driven by bake-offs on proprietary documents.
insights.quote: I think at the end of the day, the thing that matters most is for people to try things on their own documents.

insights.claim: For low-margin-of-error domains like healthcare, Reducto emphasizes traceability (where each value was extracted from) and accurate confidence scoring so humans know what to review, since perfect accuracy is unattainable.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Confidence calibration and citations are key buying criteria in regulated verticals.
insights.quote: there's never going to be a line for truly perfect.

insights.claim: Reducto benchmarks not only extraction accuracy but how reliably it escalates imperfect results to a human reviewer.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Escalation reliability is an underappreciated metric for human-in-the-loop AI.
insights.quote: We say like of the things that weren't perfect, how reliably could we escalate to a human that this is not perfect?

insights.claim: Reducto's ML team runs continuous evaluations in production to detect imperfect outputs and identify out-of-distribution failure patterns (e.g., handwriting on a tilted page outside grid lines) that feed the next training run.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Production volume becomes a data flywheel for the long tail.
insights.quote: our ML team puts a lot of time into continuous evaluations.

insights.claim: At one point Reducto had more data labelers than full-time employees.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows heavy investment in labeled data as a moat for document-specialized models.
insights.quote: at some point we had more data labelers than we had full-time employees.

insights.claim: Reducto chose a horizontal rather than vertical document platform, arguing documents boil down to shared primitives (semantic blocks, table structure), so robustness on faxed healthcare tables transfers to finance customers.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Horizontal doc-AI can serve the hardest cases across verticals, at the cost of being a harder build.
insights.quote: a lot of documents ultimately boil down to very similar primitives.

insights.claim: Adit wants objective tasks like parsing to be horizontal and zero-shot, while subjective tasks (e.g., a finance team's metric definitions) should be promptable and steerable.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Defines product boundary between commodity parsing and customer-tuned extraction.
insights.quote: we want that to be horizontal we want that to be zero shot

insights.claim: Adit sees defensibility in continuous evals over a billion pages per month and broadening customer intuition, but frames the market as meritocratic where AI-native customers like Harvey will switch if Reducto is not the best.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Doc-parsing moats are thin; execution speed, not lock-in, determines share.
insights.quote: if we don't continue being the best like they will look for the best themselves.

insights.claim: Reducto focuses on actions on documents (parsing, classification, editing) and is not interested in adjacent areas like file storage unless it improves customer experience.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Reducto is unlikely to compete with storage/content-management incumbents near term.
insights.quote: we care the most about the actual actions with the document itself.

insights.claim: A Reducto legal-tech customer found end users interacted with documents twice as much when parsed by Reducto, because answer quality and citation precision improved.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Parsing quality has measurable downstream engagement effects for AI application vendors.
insights.quote: one of our legal tech customers ended up finding that customers interact with documents twice as much >> when it's parsed by reducto.

insights.claim: Adit argues RAG has not died: most agent products, including agents crawling file systems, are still search plus inference over results, which is definitionally retrieval augmented generation.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Retrieval infrastructure stays relevant even as long-context and agentic file search rise.
insights.quote: a lot of problems ultimately are search problems

themes.theme: White-collar 'Claude Code moment' and document editing

insights.claim: Adit believes white-collar work has not yet had its equivalent of a Claude Code moment, and that work ends with writing into spreadsheets and Word docs, motivating Reducto's push into editing.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Document write/edit automation is an emerging AI category beyond extraction.
insights.quote: I don't think white collar work has quite had the equivalence of like um a quad code moment.

insights.claim: Reducto aims to let models redline contracts and fill out loan applications reliably; it launched a form-editing endpoint about six months ago and says upcoming releases will be a step-function change.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Watch for Reducto editing product launches entering legal and lending workflows.
insights.quote: We launched a form editing endpoint not too long ago. um close to like 6 months at this point.

insights.claim: Adit says humans spend billions of dollars per year on document localization, where models translate well but applying edits (e.g., English to right-to-left Arabic with reflowed layout) remains hard and manual.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Document localization is a large, under-automated market Reducto is targeting.
insights.quote: humans spend billions of dollars per year on document localization.

insights.claim: Adit argues model intelligence is now roughly sufficient for white-collar automation; the bottleneck is fragmented enterprise data and undocumented institutional heuristics, since frontier labs hill-climbed on verifiable codegen first.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Value accrues to tooling that aggregates context and knowledge bases, not just smarter models.
insights.quote: models have gotten so good at long horizon reasoning that it feels less and less likely that intelligence is the biggest bottleneck.

insights.claim: Adit names vertical AI customers Basis (automating tax filing), Harvey and Lora (legal, as transcribed) as partners that figure out end-to-end value delivery in their contexts.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Reducto is infrastructure beneath leading vertical AI apps.

insights.claim: Reducto hired Leang (as transcribed), who went viral on Twitter for open-source office agents and moved from Singapore, to lead its document editing work.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Signals seriousness of Reducto's editing push.

insights.claim: Reducto's sales team grew from one AE at the start of the year to about 30 people, with roughly 40 roles open and the team still feeling capacity constrained.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Indicates strong demand and rapid go-to-market scaling post-Series B.
insights.quote: Like we still feel capacity constrained as a team.

insights.claim: Reducto's sales team heavily uses Devin to build custom prospect websites and uses Claude design for proposals instead of Google Slides, adopted bottom-up rather than mandated.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Coding agents are diffusing into non-engineering functions like sales.
insights.quote: our sales team now uses Devon a ton.

insights.claim: Reducto has allowed LLM use in interviews since day one and runs full-day 8-hour onsites designed to be hard to solve without using LLMs properly.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: AI-tool fluency is becoming an explicit hiring filter at AI startups.
insights.quote: allowed LLM and on-sites since day one

insights.claim: Reducto's top cultural value is obsession with one's craft, assessed by asking candidates about something they are world class at, including hobbies like video games.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Hiring for obsession over credentials as a scaling culture lever.
insights.quote: our number one cultural value is having obsession for your craft

insights.claim: Adit has shifted from weekly priorities to monthly and quarterly priorities but avoids annual OKRs because the market changes too quickly.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Planning horizons stay short at fast-growing AI startups.
insights.quote: the market changes so quickly today that if you don't adjust as a function of whatever the current thing is like you're behind

insights.claim: Reducto originated from an Anthropic hackathon with early Claude access, where context window limits led to a long-term memory product (RememberAll) before pivoting to documents during YC.
insights.speaker: Adit Abraham (Reducto CEO)
insights.so_what: Origin story: pivot from agent memory to document infrastructure.
